source.title: Conceptual capacity and effective complexity of neural networks
source.authors: Lech Szymanski; B. McCane; C. Atkinson

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Figure legends and plotted test-error values are not included in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates a new complexity measure against test error, including across networks trained with varying amounts of randomized-label data; this is a different measurement aimed at the generalization question.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own conceptual-capacity results and textual relationships with test error. The true-versus-random-label figure shows test error in its legend, but the supplied text omits those values. Cited findings from prior work are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: Section 5.2 directly repeats the natural-versus-random-label comparison, measuring training and test error for the same architectures and training recipes within each dataset pair. This bears on V1 independently of the proposed conceptual-capacity measure. The supplied text establishes zero training error but omits the held-out results needed for a verdict.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors propose conceptual capacity as effective complexity and report correlations with generalization within architectures. They qualify cross-architecture comparisons, data dependence, computational cost and limited resolution, particularly for ResNet101. Their training analysis also shows a collapse to zero conceptual capacity coinciding with lost generalization, so the relationship is not universal across training states.
record.recipe_differences: Introduces and evaluates conceptual capacity, an entropy-based measure of a network's differential concepts; it does not reproduce the listed studies' interventions or measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The relationship between conceptual capacity and test error is reported within a given architecture; ResNet101 results are noisier. Cross-architecture capacity comparisons may not indicate relative generalization.

fits_no_version.finding: Conceptual capacity is lower for natural-label-trained networks than for randomized-label-trained counterparts in every tested architecture/dataset pair.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The proposed entropy-based conceptual-capacity measure distinguishes natural-label from random-label fits within the tested architecture and dataset.

fits_no_version.finding: Within an architecture, conceptual capacity increases with test error across confusion-set conditions, including with total training-set size fixed; ResNet101 results are noisier.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Conceptual capacity correlates with test error within a fixed architecture under label-corruption interventions.

fits_no_version.finding: Lower conceptual capacity does not consistently predict better test performance across architectures; ResNet101 has lower capacity but worse test performance than VGG16.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Conceptual-capacity comparisons depend on the architectures' concept spaces.

record.problems: The supplied text omits numerical test-error values from Figures 3–6, preventing a direct assessment of the random-label versus natural-label test-error pattern. The authors report noisy ResNet101 results, warn that capacity comparisons across architectures may be misleading, and describe substantial computation and memory demands.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted due to the 60-row limit. Exact values for Figures 3–6 are absent from the supplied text.

untested.parts: The original small Inception, AlexNet, MLP and ImageNet settings are not evaluated. Natural-label performance above chance and random-label performance at chance were measured here, but cannot be assessed from the supplied figure-free text.
No width sweep beyond the zero-training-error threshold; the depth experiment changes depth and width together at approximately fixed parameter count.
No controlled convolutional-versus-fully-connected comparison or test of local connectivity.
No controlled adaptive-optimizer-versus-SGD comparison under comparable tuning.
No controlled batch-size comparison under fixed epoch budgets.
No measurement of magnitude-aware sharpness or comparison of its ranking with norm- and margin-based measures.
No removal of examples selected by memorization influence followed by retraining.

record.verdict_notes: No V1 verdict is justified without the Figure 3 held-out results. Their absence is already recorded in R5 and rows_left_out, so it is not an additional missing result. Conceptual capacity is a different construct from V7's magnitude-aware sharpness.

versions.untested_parts: The supplied text does not give the held-out accuracy or error values needed to assess whether natural-label accuracy is far above chance and randomized-label accuracy is at chance.

rows.subject: VGG16 and ResNet101
rows.size_stated: VGG16: 33.6 million parameters; ResNet101: 42.7 million parameters
rows.operation_detail: Compared conceptual capacity for networks trained on true labels and randomized-label variants.
rows.measure: Test error; the figure caption says percentage test error is shown in the legend.
rows.note: The supplied text does not include the legend values or a textual description of the test-error comparison. The textual result concerns conceptual capacity, not held-out accuracy.
rows.check: Zero training error is explicitly established for both architectures on both natural-label and randomized-label datasets, but test-error legend values are unavailable. Split this aggregate into architecture × dataset × label-condition rows. Appendix A.2 also reports restarting unsuccessful runs with new initial weights, so the zero-error result describes successful runs rather than universal convergence.
